tweets.text:
THE DIGNITY OF THE PRESIDENCY IS GONE

It began with the Finance Bill and slowly unraveled through protest after protest, headline after headline, as the public mood shifted from silent frustration to something louder and more public. The chants started with youth, then moved into homes, workplaces, and now even classrooms, where children have joined in singing that Ruto must go.

This kind of thing doesn’t happen in a country where the presidency still means something. When the head of state becomes the subject of viral jokes, schoolyard songs, and roadside memes, it's a clear sign that the office has lost its grip on public respect.

Now we’ve reached a moment that can’t be laughed off. A shoe was thrown at the president during a public event in Migori. It may seem like a small act, but in many cultures, including ours, that gesture carries deep meaning. It is not just a form of protest, it is the ultimate sign of insult. Throwing a shoe doesn’t start dialogue or debate, it declares that the person on the receiving end is beneath contempt, undeserving of eye contact or even words.

Moments like these do not come from nowhere. They are a reflection of what people feel deep down but have not always had the courage to say out loud. Now that fear is gone. What remains is mockery, disgust, and a presidency that no longer commands anything beyond armored convoys and heavy police presence.

There is an example history does not forget. In 1999, Boris Yeltsin, then the President of Russia, went on national television and shocked the world by resigning from office. He admitted that he had let the Russian people down. He said the country needed new energy, new leadership, and that clinging to power would only drag the nation deeper into shame. His decision came at a time when public trust was gone and Russia had become an international punchline. That resignation, painful as it was, helped reset the national image and gave the institution of the presidency a chance to recover.

If Ruto cares at all about the office he holds, and about the future of the country he leads, then this is the moment to reflect. Because when citizens reach the point of throwing shoes, and when children no longer associate the presidency with pride, then we are far beyond politics. We are dealing with something broken. And the only thing that can restore it might be the one thing no president ever wants to consider.

tweets.text:
This is quite consequential.

China, Japan, South Korea and the countries of ASEAN just issued a joint statement (https://t.co/CyiMeQ4GZ6) in which they take a unified stance against "escalating trade protectionism", a clear reference to Trump's tariffs.

They write that their common "policy priority" is "to reinforce long-term resilience" of the region, which given the policies they detail clearly means building financial and trade infrastructure that aims at reducing their exposure to the US. 

The statement outlines a comprehensive strategy to strengthen trade between the signatories, enhance local currency bond markets and reduce dependence on Western financial institutions (via, for instance, the expansion of the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation, CMIM). 

Particularly notable is their explicit support for the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) - the world's largest trade agreement that includes all the signatories but not the US.

All in all, Trump is achieving the unthinkable: bringing East and Southeast Asia together in an economic bloc that seeks to derisk itself from America.
